steps.stem: Researchers gave each of the participants in an experiment a box of chocolates. Half of the participants were told that the chocolates had been made by hand in a small workshop, and the other half were told that they had been made in a large factory. In fact, the chocolates in all the boxes were the same. After tasting them, each participant rated how tasty the chocolates were. Which of the following hypotheses did the researchers test?
choices: People prefer chocolates that are sold in a box to chocolates that are sold loose
What people are told about how a food was made influences how tasty it seems to them
Food that is made by hand in small workshops is tastier than food that is made in large factories
People who taste a food before rating it rate it higher than people who do not taste it
explanation: The only thing that differs between the two halves is what they were told about how the chocolates were made, and what is measured is how tasty they seemed. The chocolates themselves were the same, so (3), which is about real differences between the chocolates, is not what was tested; everyone received a box (1) and everyone tasted (4).

steps.stem: For many years, the farmers of a certain village believed that the dark spots that appear on the figs in their orchards are caused by the morning fog, and that the tiny wasps found in the orchards in the same season play no part in this. Later observations showed that this belief was wrong. Which of the following results would not have shown that the belief was wrong?
choices: Figs that were picked and eaten before the season of fog did not have spots
In a year in which the wasps did not reach the orchards because of a late frost, there were almost no spots, although the fog was as usual
In an orchard on the slope of the mountain, where there is never morning fog, many of the figs had spots
A farmer who covered part of his trees with fine nets found spots only on the trees that were not covered
explanation: Figs picked before the season of fog are not what the belief is about: with no fog, the belief also predicts no spots, so this result fits it. (2) shows fog without spots when the wasps were absent, (3) shows spots without fog, and (4) shows that the nets, which kept the wasps away but not the fog, prevented the spots.

steps.stem: A study found that when background music is played, people perform repetitive tasks better than they do in silence, whereas they perform tasks that require careful reading worse than they do in silence. Which of the following hypotheses does not explain this finding?
choices: Music arouses the listener. Arousal prevents the sleepiness that monotonous work causes, but it disturbs the concentration that careful reading requires
Listening to music uses the same abilities that are used in reading, and therefore music disturbs reading, while in monotonous work the music reduces boredom
Music draws part of the attention away from the task, and this harms the performance of every task, but in a monotonous task, which requires little attention, the harm is smaller
Music improves the mood, and a good mood helps in simple tasks but causes people to read less carefully
explanation: A harm that is smaller in monotonous tasks is still a harm, so it cannot explain why these tasks are performed better with music than in silence. (1), (2) and (4) each give a reason for both halves of the finding.

steps.stem: The ecologist Harari counted, over twelve years, the nests of terns in two parts of an island: on the cliffs of its northern coast and on the sandy shore of its southern coast. She found that there are many more nests on the cliffs than on the shore, and that the difference between the two parts changes from year to year: a rise in the number of foxes on the island hardly affects the number of nests on the cliffs, but leads to a sharp drop in the number of nests on the shore. According to her findings, if there were more foxes on the island in 1987 than in 1986, it is likely that -
choices: the number of nests on the cliffs in 1987 was lower than in 1986
the number of nests on the shore in 1987 was higher than the number of nests on the cliffs in that year
in 1987 the number of nests on the shore was the same as in 1986, but on the cliffs it was much lower
the gap in the number of nests between the cliffs and the shore was greater in 1987 than in 1986
explanation: More foxes leave the cliffs almost unchanged and cut the shore sharply, so the gap grows. (1) changes the part that foxes hardly affect, (3) swaps the roles of the two parts, and (2) contradicts the finding that the cliffs have far more nests, which is even truer after a rise in foxes.

steps.stem: Researchers who followed a certain desert shrub for several years found that its seeds, which are covered with a hard coat, germinate only after they have passed through the digestive system of a gazelle, which softens the coat. The shrub bears fruit once a year, at the beginning of summer, and the fruit falls to the ground within about three weeks. Gazelles prefer to eat grass, and they eat the fruit of the shrub only when grass is hard to find. Based on the paragraph, in which of the following years is it most likely that many new shrubs will begin to grow?
choices: A year in which the shrubs bore more fruit than usual
A year in which there was little grass at the end of winter
A year in which there was little grass at the beginning of summer
A year in which there were more gazelles in the area than in other years
explanation: Seeds germinate only after a gazelle has eaten the fruit, gazelles eat it only when grass is scarce, and the fruit is there only in early summer. (2) has scarce grass at a time when there is no fruit, and (1) and (4) are a step short: with plenty of grass, the gazelles would not eat the fruit.

steps.title: Scientific reasoning — the words to know
steps.intro: Every study follows one chain: hypothesis → experiment → results → conclusion.

head: Term
What it means
rows: Cause and effect: if X changes, Y changes
X = the factor we change · Y = the result we measure
Groups identical except X — otherwise an alternative explanation
The comparison group: X absent, or X at a different level
The result — supports the hypothesis or contradicts it
Why the results came out as they did

tips: Two question types: understanding the study · understanding the findings.
Assumptions: flip it — if the opposite would ruin the experiment, it's an assumption.
Conclusions given: work out what must follow before reading the choices.
An explanation must cover every part of the finding.

steps.stem: The skin of the Galapagos shark stays remarkably free of algae and barnacles, although no toxic substance has been found in it. Its tiny scales form a pattern of fine ridges, and surfaces imprinted with a similar pattern have been found to make it difficult for bacteria to attach to them and settle on them. In hospitals, surfaces are kept clean with disinfectants, which must be applied again and again, and some bacteria develop resistance to them. According to the paragraph, which of the following new ways of keeping hospital surfaces free of bacteria could develop as a result of this finding?
choices: Extracting the substance that protects the shark's skin from algae and barnacles and adding it to disinfectants
Adding disinfectants to the material from which door handles and bed rails are made, so that there is no need to apply them again and again and the bacteria do not have time to develop resistance
Applying disinfectants in a pattern of fine ridges, so that they cover the surface more efficiently
Making door handles and bed rails whose surface is imprinted with a pattern like that of the shark's skin, instead of disinfecting them again and again
explanation: The finding is protection that works through the shape of the surface, not through any substance; only (4) uses it. (1) relies on a substance that, according to the paragraph, has not been found in the skin, (2) keeps the disinfectants, and (3) uses the pattern only as a way of applying them.

steps.stem: In a study, employees of a large company, some of whom walk to work and some of whom drive, were asked to list the names of the streets along the route between their home and their workplace. Two findings emerged from the study. First, the employees who walk named the streets along their route far more accurately than the employees who drive. Second, on their way to work, the employees who walk look at street signs much more often than the employees who drive. What is the relationship between the two findings?
choices: The second finding can explain the first finding
The first finding proves the second finding
The two findings contradict each other
The second finding is a particular case of the first finding
explanation: Looking at street signs more often accounts for knowing the street names better, so the second finding explains the first. (2) reverses the direction, (3) sees a conflict where there is none, and (4) treats two different measures as a rule and an example of it.

steps.stem: A study of the market for used farm machinery in a certain country found that a tractor bought two years earlier was usually sold for only slightly less than the current price of a new tractor of the same model, whereas a combine harvester bought two years earlier sold for much less than the current price of a new combine of the same model. Which of the following could explain these findings?
choices: Two years ago new combines cost much more than new tractors, but since then their price has fallen, and it is still falling
In the two years before the study, the price of new tractors fell considerably, while the price of new combines hardly changed
Most buyers of used combines are small farms that cannot afford to buy a new one
Combines wear out with use more slowly than tractors, so a two-year-old combine is usually in better condition than a tractor of the same age
explanation: If new tractors have become much cheaper, a used tractor is compared with today's low price, so the gap is small; combine prices did not fall, so their gap stays wide. (1) has the wrong machine getting cheaper, (3) does not explain the difference between the two machines, and (4) would narrow the gap for combines rather than widen it.

steps.stem: Professor Gorlitz said of a certain study: "It is like trying to find out whether the passengers on a bus arrive rested at their destination, by checking how tired the driver is at the end of the day." Which of the following is most likely to be the study to which Professor Gorlitz was referring?
choices: A study that examined whether the residents of a certain neighborhood sleep better since the road near their homes was closed to traffic, in which the residents were asked how they had slept before the closure and after it

A study on the question of whether cookery programs on the radio improve the cooking of their listeners, in which the dishes of listeners were compared with the dishes of people who do not listen to such programs
A study that examined whether a certain cookery program on the radio improves the cooking of its listeners, by comparing the dishes of the program's presenters with the dishes of other cooks
A study on the effect of a new mattress, in which people who had bought it were asked, a year later, whether their back pain had lessened
explanation: The comparison faults a study that examines those who provide something instead of those who receive it: the presenters stand to the listeners as the driver stands to the passengers. (1), (2) and (4) examine the very people the question is about, whatever their other weaknesses.

steps.stem: Researchers found that mice kept in cages with a running wheel did better on memory tasks than mice kept in identical cages without a wheel, and that the blood of the running mice contained higher levels of a certain protein that muscles produce during exercise. The researchers hypothesized that this protein, carried by the blood to the brain, is what improves memory. To test their hypothesis, they repeated the experiment with a single change. Which of the following is most likely to be that change?
choices: They placed in the cages without a wheel a substance known to improve memory
They used mice of a strain with especially large muscles, which produce more of the protein during exercise
They replaced the running wheels with wheels that are harder to turn
They gave the mice in the cages with a wheel a substance that keeps the protein from reaching the brain
explanation: If mice that run but whose brains receive no protein lose their advantage in memory, the protein is the link. (1) changes only the mice that do not run, and (2) and (3) change the amount of exercise or muscle, not the path of the protein to the brain.

steps.stem: Archaeologists who examined skeletons from a Bronze Age settlement found that there was almost no decay in the inhabitants' teeth. Since the water of the settlement's spring is rich in fluoride, the archaeologists concluded that drinking this water protected the inhabitants' teeth. Another researcher argued that people in that period ate almost no sugar, and that their teeth would have been healthy in any case. Which of the following findings could weaken the other researcher's argument?
choices: Skeletons from the same period from a nearby settlement, whose spring water contains almost no fluoride, with a high rate of tooth decay
Skeletons from the same settlement from the Roman period, when honey was common in the diet, whose teeth are mostly decayed although the spring was still in use
Remains of many clay jars near the spring
Plant remains showing that the inhabitants ate mainly barley and lentils
explanation: People of the same period ate as little sugar, yet without fluoride their teeth decayed, so the diet alone does not explain the healthy teeth. (2) points to sugar as the cause and fits the other researcher, (3) at most shows that the spring was used, and (4) fits his argument.

steps.stem: Researchers who studied a certain songbird found that there are fewer aphids on bushes in which the birds nest than on other bushes. According to one hypothesis, the birds feed aphids to their chicks and thus reduce their numbers. According to another hypothesis, the birds prefer from the start to nest in bushes with few aphids, because the sticky honeydew that aphids secrete fouls their feathers. Which of the following tests could decide between the two hypotheses?
choices: Covering some of the bushes with nets that birds cannot pass through, and comparing the number of aphids on them with the number on bushes that were not covered
Moving nests with chicks in them to bushes chosen without regard to the number of aphids on them, and counting the aphids on these bushes a few weeks later
Counting the aphids on bushes in which birds of other species have nested
Examining the food that the parents bring to the chicks
explanation: When the bushes are chosen without regard to aphids, the birds' preference plays no part: if these bushes lose their aphids, the birds are the cause. In (1) the uncovered bushes include those the birds chose, (3) says nothing about this bird's choice, and (4) at most shows that the birds eat aphids, not why their bushes have few.

steps.stem: More than ninety percent of the world's adults carry the Epstein-Barr virus, but only a small proportion of them have ever had mononucleosis, a disease that this virus causes. Which of the following could explain these facts?
choices: Mononucleosis appears in everyone who has carried the virus for more than a few years
The virus passes from person to person mainly through saliva, and most people are infected with it before the age of thirty
Mononucleosis is caused by the virus together with a certain bacterium that almost all adults also carry, usually from early childhood
Mononucleosis develops mainly in people who were first infected with the virus as adolescents or adults, and most people are infected as young children
explanation: A virus that causes the disease mainly under a condition that most carriers do not meet fits a virus that nearly everyone carries and a disease that few have had. (1) and (3) would make the disease almost universal, and (2) explains only why so many carry the virus, not why so few have had the disease.

steps.stem: Researchers who study the young of a certain desert lizard offered each young lizard, in a series of trials, two beetles: one of a species that secretes a foul-tasting liquid, and an edible beetle of similar size. In most of the trials the lizards ate the edible beetle. The researchers hypothesized that the lizards could tell the two beetles apart before the experiment began, and did not learn to do so during it. Which of the following findings would support their hypothesis?
choices: Larger lizards ate the edible beetle more often than smaller lizards did
In the first trials the lizards ate both kinds of beetle about equally often, but a lizard that had once tasted the foul-tasting beetle did not touch it again
The lizards chose the edible beetle in their first trials no less often than in their last trials
Lizards that ate the foul-tasting beetle were not harmed
explanation: Learning during the experiment would show as improvement from the first trials to the last; no improvement points to an ability the lizards already had. (2) describes learning, (1) compares lizards with one another rather than early trials with late ones, and (4) does not bear on the hypothesis.

steps.stem: Farmers in a river valley have noticed that in the two or three years after a winter in which the river overflows its banks, the fields near the river yield larger wheat crops than usual, after which the yield returns to its normal level. An agronomist attributes this to the layer of silt that the flood leaves on the fields. Which of the following does not strengthen his explanation?
choices: The silt left by the river contains a large amount of nitrogen, which the soil of these fields lacks and which wheat needs in order to grow well
In the years after a flood there are almost no voles, which eat young wheat plants, in the fields near the river, because many of them drowned
In a field near the river whose owner scraped away the silt immediately after the flood, the yield was no larger than usual
The nitrogen in the silt is gradually washed down into the deeper layers of the soil
explanation: The drowned voles offer another reason for the larger crops, one that has nothing to do with the silt. (1) gives the silt a way of helping the wheat, (3) shows no effect where the silt was removed, and (4) explains why the effect of the silt fades.

steps.stem: Root-knot nematodes are tiny worms that live inside the roots of tomato plants, where many chemical pesticides do not reach them. Nevertheless, some growers reduce their numbers by growing French marigolds in a field for one season before planting tomatoes in it. Which of the following could explain why growing marigolds is effective against root-knot nematodes?
choices: The roots of the marigold release into the soil a substance that is toxic to the worms
Marigolds attract bees, which pollinate the flowers of the tomato plants
The smell of the marigolds drives away insects that feed on nematodes
Marigolds lower the concentration of pesticides in the soil, so that they do less damage to the roots of the tomato plants
explanation: Only (1) links the marigolds to the death of the worms. (3) would actually help the worms, and (2) and (4) concern pollination and pesticides.

steps.stem: In a study of memory for songs, Hebrew speakers listened once to songs they did not know and then sang them from memory. Some of the songs were in Hebrew and some in Hungarian, a language none of the participants knew. The participants remembered the Hebrew songs much better. The researchers attributed this mainly to understanding the language, but pointed out another possibility: the Hungarian songs that had been chosen were longer than the Hebrew ones. A second experiment showed that the length of the songs is of little importance. Which of the following is most likely to be the result of the second experiment?
choices: Participants who do not understand Hebrew remembered Hebrew songs and Hungarian songs equally well
The participants remembered songs they had performed in the past better than songs they had only heard
The participants remembered long Hebrew songs better than short Hungarian songs
The participants learned short songs faster than long songs, whatever the language
explanation: Only (3) sets the two factors against each other: long Hebrew songs still beat short Hungarian ones, so length matters little. (4) shows that length does matter, (2) is about having performed a song, not its length, and (1) concerns people who understand neither language.

steps.stem: A study compared the success rates in the final examinations of two high schools in a certain European city. In school A, a larger proportion of the students passed the examinations than in school B. However, when the students were divided into those who had studied at the advanced level and those who had studied at the basic level, it was found that at each level the proportion of students who passed in school B was no smaller than in school A. Which of the following could explain these findings?
choices: The advanced-level examinations in school A are harder than those in school B, because in school A they include an additional part that is not required in school B
In each of the schools, the number of students at the advanced level was equal to the number at the basic level
In both schools, most of the students who passed the examinations had studied at the basic level
Most of the students in school B studied at the advanced level, at which fewer students pass the examinations, while in school A most studied at the basic level
explanation: If school B does no worse at either level but worse overall, most of its students must be at the level where fewer pass. (1) would lower school A's results, not raise them, (2) would make the overall rates follow the rates at each level, and (3) describes where the successful students studied in both schools alike.

steps.stem: Honey is a supersaturated solution of sugars, mainly glucose and fructose. Glucose dissolves in water less readily than fructose, and when there is a great deal of it relative to the water, it separates from the solution as crystals. Acacia honey, in which the proportion of fructose is especially high, stays liquid for years, whereas rapeseed honey crystallizes within a few days. According to the paragraph, which of the following could explain why rapeseed honey crystallizes quickly?
choices: It contains a high proportion of glucose relative to its water content
Rapeseed flowers in cold regions
The sugars in it do not stay dissolved for long
Like acacia honey, it contains both glucose and fructose, as well as a little water
explanation: According to the paragraph, crystals form when there is much glucose relative to the water, so a high proportion of glucose explains the quick crystallization. (3) restates the fact instead of explaining it, (4) is true of acacia honey as well, and (2) brings in a factor the paragraph does not mention.

steps.stem: In several hospital wards, a large sign reminding the staff to wash their hands was hung above every sink. In the first weeks, the rate of hand washing rose considerably, but after about four months it returned to its previous level. Which of the following best explains these findings?
choices: When the signs were hung, the wards also switched to a soap that dries the skin less
At first the staff noticed the signs because they were new, but after a while they stopped paying attention to them
Staff members who noticed the signs washed their hands more often, and every staff member passes the sinks many times a day
About a month after the signs were hung, the wards began to hold a monthly check of hand washing
explanation: Signs that stop being noticed explain an effect that fades. (1) and (3) would predict a lasting rise, and (4) should have raised the rate further, not lowered it.

steps.stem: A man claims that when he walks across a field holding a forked stick, he can tell where water flows beneath the ground. A researcher wished to test his claim. Which of the following tests is the most suitable for this purpose?
choices: The man will walk across the same field twice, a week apart, and the researcher will check whether he points to the same places both times
Another person who claims to have the same ability will walk across the field without having seen the first man do so, and the researcher will compare the places to which the two of them point
The man will walk across a field in which there is a well, and will be asked whether there is water under the well
Several pipes will be buried under a field, and each time water will flow through one of them, chosen by the researcher without the man's knowledge; the man will be asked to point to it
explanation: Only a test in which the answer is known to the researcher and hidden from the man can show whether he really senses the water. Anyone can repeat the same answers in (1), (2) compares two claims that have not been tested, and in (3) the well gives the answer away.

steps.stem: A study of the work of professional tasters found that they identify sourness more accurately in the morning than in the afternoon, while they identify sweetness more accurately in the afternoon than in the morning. Following these findings, several recommendations were made to a juice factory. Which of the following recommendations is not consistent with the findings of the study?
choices: Tasters who check whether a juice is too sweet should do so in the afternoon
The hour at which juice is tasted should be determined according to what the taster is checking
Since lemon juice is mainly sour, the sweetness of new kinds of lemon juice should be checked in the morning
A juice that was found in the afternoon to be less sour than required should be tasted again in the morning before its recipe is changed
explanation: Sweetness is identified better in the afternoon, whatever the juice; the fact that lemon juice is sour does not change that. (1), (2) and (4) follow from the findings.

steps.stem: At a summer camp, the children are served juice every morning in red cups and in blue cups, and each child takes one cup. The red cups are always placed on the table nearer the door. Ronit, one of the counselors, noticed that most of the children take red cups, and assumed that they prefer the color red. The camp director suspected another reason, and an experiment carried out the next day showed that Ronit's assumption was wrong. Which of the following best describes the experiment and its result?
choices: The blue cups were placed on the table nearer the door and the red cups on the other table, and most of the children took blue cups
The red cups were placed farther from the children than the blue cups, and most of the children still took red cups
Only blue cups were served, and almost all the children agreed to drink from them
The children were offered red cups and green cups, and most of them took red ones
explanation: When the colors change places and the children follow the place, not the color, the preference for red is ruled out. (2) and (4) fit a preference for red, and (3) does not test preference at all.

steps.stem: In an experiment, participants were asked to choose, from twelve reproductions of paintings, the one they liked best. Some of the participants were then told, falsely, that most of the other participants had chosen the same painting, and the others were told that hardly anyone had chosen it. Finally, each participant was asked how much they would be willing to pay for a print of the painting they had chosen. Which of the following is most likely to have been the purpose of the experiment?
choices: To examine how the price of a print affects the chance that people will choose it
To examine whether people tend to choose the paintings that others have chosen
To examine whether the value people attach to an object they chose depends on whether their choice seems unusual or common
To examine whether choosing one painting out of many increases people's willingness to buy it, even for more than it is worth
explanation: The only thing varied is whether the choice seems common or unusual, and the only thing measured is how much the participant would pay. (1) reverses cause and effect, (2) concerns the choice, which was made before the information was given, and (4) names something that was the same for everyone.

steps.stem: A reader wrote to the editor of a local weekly: "Every year more amateur theater groups perform in our area, and surely not all of them are good. How is it, then, that almost every review of a play in your paper is favorable?" Which of the following could explain the situation she describes?
choices: The paper's critics often disagree among themselves about which plays are good
The editor is of the opinion that bad plays should be criticized severely, so that the public will not waste money on them
The paper's critics write only about the plays they recommend to readers
The paper devotes more space to reviews of plays today than it did in the past
explanation: If the critics write only about plays they liked, the reviews will be favorable however many poor plays are performed. (2) predicts the opposite, and (1) and (4) do not explain why the reviews lean toward praise.

steps.stem: In an experiment, two groups of participants tasted the same soup and rated its saltiness. One group tasted it while loud music was playing, and the other in a quiet room. The participants in the first group were then asked whether the music had affected their rating, and most of them said that it had not affected it at all. However, the first group rated the soup as considerably less salty than the second group did. Which of the following is most likely to have been the purpose of the experiment?
choices: To examine whether people consider their own sense of taste better than that of others
To examine whether loud music makes food taste less salty
To examine whether people whose attention is distracted by music or by conversation rate the food they are eating more highly
To examine whether people are aware of the way in which the noise around them affects their judgment of taste
explanation: The experiment sets what the participants said the music did against what it actually did. (2) covers only the comparison between the groups and ignores the question put to the first group, and (1) and (3) are not tested at all.

steps.stem: A bakery has two branches, and in each of them bread is baked in two shifts, a day shift and a night shift. At one of the branches, the owner noticed that more loaves are burnt in the day shift, which Sima manages, than in the night shift, and told Sima that he intends to replace her. Sima claimed that the burnt loaves are not her fault, and asked him to look into a certain matter before he decides. Which of the following is most likely to be that matter?
choices: Whether the ovens have recently been breaking down more often than in the past
Whether at the other branch, too, more loaves are burnt in the day shift than in the night shift
Whether the flour the bakery has been buying recently is of lower quality than before
Whether the manager of the night shift has been managing it longer than Sima has been managing the day shift, and whether he has more experience in baking
explanation: If the other branch also burns more loaves by day, the shift and not the manager explains the difference. The ovens (1) and the flour (3) serve both shifts alike, and (4) would point to Sima's shorter experience rather than clear her.

steps.stem: A survey of beekeepers and of other residents of several farming villages found that allergy to bee stings is far less common among the beekeepers than among the other residents. The authors of the survey concluded that keeping bees reduces the risk of developing such an allergy. Which of the following could be an alternative explanation for the survey's findings?
choices: People who are allergic to bee stings generally avoid keeping bees
Beekeepers are stung by bees much more often than other people
Beekeepers who wear protective suits are stung less often than beekeepers who do not
Frequent stings gradually accustom the body not to react severely to the venom
explanation: The allergy may keep people away from beekeeping rather than beekeeping preventing the allergy. (4) is a way in which the survey's own conclusion could work, and (2) and (3) do not explain why beekeepers are less often allergic.

steps.stem: A veterinarian noticed that in the week after a holiday on which bonfires are lit, more dogs than usual are brought to his clinic with burns on their paws. He suspected that the dogs had stepped on embers left from the bonfires, and found that about seventy percent of the dogs brought to him with burns had been taken by their owners to a bonfire. The answer to which of the following questions will help him determine whether his suspicion is justified?
choices: What proportion of the burned dogs were burned at night?
What proportion of the dogs in the area that were not burned had been taken to a bonfire?
How many of the dogs that were taken to a bonfire were not burned?
What proportion of the dogs that were taken to a bonfire were puppies, whose paws are more sensitive than those of grown dogs?
explanation: Seventy percent means something only if it is higher than the proportion of unhurt dogs that were taken to a bonfire. (3) gives a number with nothing to compare it with, and (1) and (4) do not bear on the suspicion.

steps.stem: At gymnastics competitions, judges give on average higher scores to gymnasts from well-known clubs. According to one explanation, the judges are influenced by the reputation of these clubs. According to another explanation, gymnasts from well-known clubs are simply better trained. Which of the following studies is most likely to determine which of the two explanations is correct?
choices: Comparing the average scores of gymnasts from well-known clubs with those of gymnasts from small clubs
Asking the judges whether they know which club each gymnast belongs to
Checking the number of weekly training hours at well-known clubs and at small clubs, and the qualifications of the coaches at each of them
Comparing the scores of gymnasts who moved from a small club to a well-known one in competitions held shortly before the move and shortly after it
explanation: Shortly after the move, the gymnast's training has hardly changed, but the club's name has; a rise in scores would support the first explanation and no rise the second. Both explanations predict (1), (3) supports the second without ruling out the first, and (2) does not show whether knowing the club affects the scores.

steps.stem: Researchers gave two groups of participants a story about a grocer who sold cheese that had gone bad, after which seven of his customers fell ill. Group A was told that the grocer had not known that the cheese had gone bad, and group B was told that he had known and sold it anyway. The researchers hypothesized that when a person is regarded as more to blame for an act, people tend to remember the act as more serious than it really was. Which of the following findings supports the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: When asked how many customers had fallen ill, the members of group A gave, on average, about the number in the story, and the members of group B a much larger number
More members of group A than of group B remembered what kind of cheese had been sold
Most of the members of group B, but only a few of the members of group A, thought that the grocer should be fined
More members of group B than of group A remembered, mistakenly, that the story said the grocer had apologized to his customers and compensated them for the damage
explanation: The grocer seen as more to blame is remembered as having made more people ill. (4) is a memory error that makes the act less serious, (3) is a judgment, not a memory, and (2) does not concern the seriousness of the act.

steps.stem: A school principal found that students who chose to join the school's chess club received, on average, higher grades in mathematics than the other students, and concluded that playing chess improves students' ability in mathematics. The mathematics coordinator argued that her conclusion is not justified, since students who are good at mathematics are more likely than others to choose to join a chess club. In which of the following cases can the conclusion be criticized in the same way?
choices: A dairy farmer gave a new feed to the cows in one of his two cowsheds, which are identical, and these cows gave more milk than the others; he concluded that the new feed increases milk production

Residents of a certain town who chose to join a morning walking group run by the local council have, on average, lower blood pressure than the other residents; the council concluded that walking lowers blood pressure
People who sleep more are, on average, less irritable than people who sleep less; a psychologist concluded that Yigal, who sleeps more than his brother, is probably less irritable than he is

Most of the passengers of a certain bus company said in a survey that it is the most punctual company in the country, and the company concluded from this that no other bus company in the country is more punctual than it is
explanation: People who choose to walk every morning may be the ones who take care of their health anyway, just as good students choose the chess club. In (1) the cows did not choose the feed, (3) draws no conclusion about a cause, and (4) has a different flaw.
